curation.lead:
The International Peace Institute (IPI), a New York-based think tank registered as a 501(c)(3) under EIN 03-0213226, served as one of the primary institutional conduits through which Jeffrey Epstein channeled influence over international diplomacy and foreign policy. Under the presidency of Norwegian diplomat Terje Rod-Larsen, IPI received at least $650,000 in KPMG-confirmed Epstein conduit funds and an additional $5.86 million in Epstein-directed funding, while simultaneously drawing on sovereign donors including the Norwegian and Swedish governments (Finding #1182). IPI operated a Mongolia Advisory Board that paid $100,000 each to former heads of state including Rod-Larsen, Lawrence Summers, Ehud Barak, and Kevin Rudd, effectively creating a parallel diplomatic apparatus funded through opaque channels (Finding #1147).

Financial analysis of IPI's 990 filings from 2010 through 2023 reveals a steep institutional decline that correlates with Epstein's exposure and arrest. Peak assets of $18.6 million in 2010 fell to $4.9 million by 2023, a 73% collapse. The organization ran cumulative deficits of $14.5 million over this period, with expenses exceeding revenue in every year except 2010 and 2021 (Findings #421, #458). An anomalous $8 million deficit in 2011 suggests a major financial disruption that predated public Epstein scrutiny and warrants further examination (Finding #468).

Despite receiving funding from foreign governments and engaging extensively with U.S. Congressional members on its advisory boards, IPI has no registration under the Foreign Agents Registration Act. Norway's own development agency (NORAD) has registered six FARA entries through other grantees, making IPI's absence from the FARA database anomalous. The combination of foreign sovereign funding, Congressional engagement, and Epstein-directed financial flows raises unresolved questions about IPI's regulatory compliance and the degree to which Epstein used the institution as a vehicle for undisclosed foreign influence operations (Findings #387, #1147).

sections.title: Network and Funding Relationships
sections.content:
IPI's financial network reveals a convergence of Epstein-linked entities, sovereign donors, and major philanthropic institutions that together provided the organization with both revenue and reputational cover. The most direct financial link ran through Enhanced Education, the trade name of J. Epstein Virgin Islands Foundation Inc. Enhanced Education donated $125,000 to IPI in October 2011 to fund a fellowship named after WK Rick Hooper, and in March 2014 reimbursed IPI $14,158.88 for a first-class flight for Lawrence Summers, totaling $139,158.88 in documented direct transfers. That the Epstein foundation was reimbursing IPI for a former U.S. Treasury Secretary's travel expenses illustrates the degree to which personal, institutional, and financial relationships had merged.

Leon Black's involvement deepened IPI's entanglement with the Epstein financial orbit. The Black Family Foundation (EIN 13-3947890) contributed funds to IPI in December 2014, according to the KPMG review, during what 990 filings show was IPI's peak revenue year of $11.87 million. Black's parallel $10.5 million pledge to Enhanced Education, structured to "avoid public disclosure of Leon name," suggests a pattern of coordinated giving through both direct and Epstein-mediated channels. Gratitude America, another Epstein-linked entity managed by Richard Kahn, granted $375,000 to IPI in 2017, further reinforcing the multi-entity conduit structure.

The Gates Foundation relationship demonstrates how Epstein positioned himself as a broker between IPI and mainstream institutional donors. IPI submitted a $20 million grant proposal to the Gates Foundation on September 4, 2013, for polio eradication work in Pakistan, Nigeria, and Somalia (EFTA02678411). The Foundation approved only $2.5 million (grant OPP1096058), signed March 2, 2014 (Finding #290). Crucially, IPI's bank wiring instructions for the $5 million Gates Foundation wire were sent to Epstein directly (EFTA02707935), indicating he served as a financial intermediary even for funds originating from legitimate philanthropic sources. Boris Nikolic, then a science advisor to Bill Gates, received IPI bank wiring instructions from Epstein in June 2013, three months before attending an IPI-Gates meeting.

The Norwegian and Swedish governments occupied a distinct role as designated "donor countries" to IPI. DOJ documents confirm that IPI staff routinely forwarded program activity reports to these sovereign donors and that Rod-Larsen directed IPI staff to provide Epstein the same reports (Finding #1182). This placed Epstein at the same informational level as sovereign government funders, an arrangement with no apparent institutional justification outside the personal relationship between Rod-Larsen and Epstein.

sections.title: Financial Trajectory and Decline
sections.content:
IPI's financial trajectory from 2010 to 2023 tells a story of institutional dependency and collapse. At its peak in 2010, IPI held $18.6 million in assets on revenue of $13.63 million. The very next year, 2011, produced an anomalous $8.07 million deficit on revenue of only $2.64 million, representing an 81% year-over-year revenue decline. This single-year collapse, which took assets from $18.6 million to $10.5 million, remains unexplained. Possible causes include a major investment loss, an accounting adjustment, or the sudden withdrawal of a very large donor. The 2011 990 PDF warrants detailed examination to determine the specific driver (Finding #468).

Following the 2011 anomaly, IPI partially recovered, reaching peak revenue of $11.87 million in 2014, the same year that both the Black Family Foundation and Enhanced Education made documented contributions. However, from 2015 onward, expenses consistently exceeded revenue, creating a structural deficit that steadily eroded the organization's reserves. The gap was persistent: $8.3 million in revenue against $9.2 million in expenses in 2015; $7.5 million against $8.5 million in 2016; $8.7 million against $8.6 million in 2017; $7.4 million against $8.6 million in 2018 (Finding #423). This pattern suggests that IPI lost access to a major funding source around 2015 and never replaced it.

The post-2019 period shows accelerating decline. Revenue fell to $3.9 million in 2020 against $5.6 million in expenses, driven by the combined effects of COVID-19 and the reputational fallout from Epstein's 2019 arrest and death. Assets collapsed to $4.9 million by 2023, representing a 73% decline from the 2010 peak. Over the full 2010 to 2023 period, IPI ran a cumulative deficit of $14.5 million, with only two years showing surpluses: 2010 and 2021. At its current burn rate of approximately $1.6 million per year in deficit spending, IPI has roughly 2.5 years of reserves remaining (Finding #458). The financial data strongly suggests that the Epstein-directed funding pipeline was not marginal to IPI's operations but structurally important to its survival.

sections.title: FARA and Regulatory Exposure
sections.content:
IPI presents a significant anomaly under the Foreign Agents Registration Act. Despite receiving funding from the Norwegian government as a confirmed "donor country," hosting 33 or more U.S. Congressional members on advisory boards, and engaging in policy advocacy that intersected with foreign government interests, IPI has zero FARA registrations. A negative search of the FARA database confirms this absence (Finding #387). Norway itself has 50 FARA-registered foreign principals, and the Norwegian Agency for Development Cooperation (NORAD) has registered six FARA entries through other U.S. grantees such as Waxman Consulting and the Center for International Policy, establishing a clear precedent that Norwegian-funded policy organizations in the United States are expected to register.

IPI could theoretically claim several FARA exemptions. Under 22 USC 611(d), the academic and scientific exemption might apply given IPI's 501(c)(3) registration as a think tank. Its charter connection to the Trygve Lie Center could support a UN affiliate exemption. And the absence of direct documented instruction from foreign governments might undercut a formal agency relationship. However, each of these defenses faces substantial counter-arguments (Finding #1147). IPI's Congressional engagement through advisory boards goes well beyond academic research. The documented evidence that Rod-Larsen directed IPI staff to send program activity reports to Epstein using the same materials "which we usually forward to donor countries like Sweden or Norway" (EFTA02675352) raises the question of whether Epstein was functioning as an undisclosed intermediary for foreign government interests.

The FARA question is not merely academic. The combination of $650,000 in KPMG-confirmed Epstein conduit funds, $5.86 million in total Epstein-directed funding, sovereign donor relationships, and Congressional advisory board activity creates a regulatory profile that is difficult to reconcile with IPI's complete absence from the FARA registry. Whether this gap reflects a deliberate strategy or institutional oversight, it represents a potential legal vulnerability that has not been publicly addressed by IPI or investigated by the Department of Justice.
